nodes.name: Constructing whole-unit measurement line plots
nodes.description: Collect length measurements to the nearest whole unit, including measurements of several objects or repeated measurements of one object. Display the measurements on an equally spaced whole-number line-plot scale, using one stacked mark per observation. Preserve numerical spacing, positions with no observations, and repeated values.
criteria: Generate a list by measuring several objects to the nearest whole unit or repeatedly measuring one object to the nearest whole unit.
Choose and label an equally spaced whole-number measurement scale that includes the observed values and retains positions for values with no observations.
Plot one mark per measurement and stack repeated values; distinguish a measurement value from its frequency and check that the plot retains every observation.

nodes.name: Measuring and plotting fractional-inch lengths
nodes.description: Generate length data using rulers marked with halves and quarters of an inch. Display the measurements on a line plot whose equally spaced horizontal scale uses appropriate whole-inch, half-inch, or quarter-inch units. Place one mark per observation and stack repeated values.
criteria: Read a ruler marked with halves or quarters of an inch and measure lengths to generate a data set.
Choose and label an equally spaced line-plot scale in whole inches, halves, or quarters that represents the measured values, retaining positions with no observations.
Plot every measurement at its numerical value, stack repeated observations, and distinguish a measured length from the number of observations at that length.

nodes.name: Plotting and adding or subtracting fractional measurements
nodes.description: Construct a line plot of measurements in halves, quarters, or eighths of a unit and use its values and frequencies to solve contextual addition and subtraction problems. Express the fractional amounts in a common plotted unit so the arithmetic uses like denominators, including whole amounts and mixed numbers when needed.
criteria: Choose and label an equally spaced scale in halves, quarters, or eighths, plot one mark per observation, and stack repeated values without omitting unobserved scale positions.
Identify the measurements and multiplicities needed for a question, and express half-, quarter-, or eighth-unit amounts with like denominators before adding or subtracting.
Use the plotted data to find and interpret a total or a difference, including the difference between the longest and shortest measured objects, and report the original measurement units.

nodes.name: Plotting fractional measurements and solving fraction-operation problems
nodes.description: Construct a line plot of measurements in halves, quarters, or eighths of a unit and solve contextual questions using its values and frequencies. Apply addition and subtraction with like or unlike denominators, fraction multiplication, and division of unit fractions by positive whole numbers or of whole numbers by unit fractions. Explain equal redistribution of a plotted fractional total with a drawing or a decomposition into unit fractions.
criteria: Construct an equally spaced line plot in halves, quarters, or eighths of a unit, retaining unobserved scale positions and stacking one mark per observation at its measured value.
Read the measurement unit, individual values, and their multiplicities to identify the quantities needed for a contextual question.
Find totals or differences from plotted measurements in whole, half, quarter or eighth units. Express the fractional parts with a common denominator and interpret the answer in the original units.
Use the data in the plot to solve a problem involving unlike denominators, fraction multiplication, or division of a whole number by a unit fraction or of a unit fraction by a positive whole number.
Find an equal share using the plotted total and the number of containers. Explain the redistribution with a drawing or a decomposition into unit fractions.

nodes.name: Measuring volume by counting unit cubes
nodes.description: A unit cube has side length one chosen length unit and volume one cubic unit. A solid filled by n such cubes without gaps or overlaps has volume n cubic units. Measure volume by packing and counting cubes, including cubes hidden in a model or drawing, and state the cubic unit used.
criteria: Explain why a packing must fill the solid without gaps or overlaps and why n unit cubes measure n cubic units.
Count all cubes in a packed solid or a sufficient drawing, using rows and layers to include hidden cubes.
Report volume in cubic centimeters, cubic inches, cubic feet, or a clearly specified improvised cube unit, distinguishing a cubic unit from a length unit.

nodes.name: Adding volumes of non-overlapping rectangular prisms
nodes.description: Find the volume of a solid composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by decomposing it into the two prisms, calculating each prism's volume from its dimensions, and adding in consistent cubic units. Shared boundary faces do not constitute an overlap of interiors.
criteria: Choose a decomposition that fills the whole solid and does not count any three-dimensional part twice.
Determine the needed dimensions of both prisms, calculate their volumes, and add them with consistent cubic units.
Explain volume additivity and use it to solve a contextual composite-solid problem.

nodes.name: Multiplication as scaling
nodes.description: Interpret multiplication of a positive quantity by a nonnegative whole number or fraction as resizing. Predict whether the product is smaller than, equal to, or larger than the positive factor from whether the multiplier is less than, equal to, or greater than one, without computing the product. Explain unchanged size under multiplication by one, including a fraction of the form n/n.
criteria: Compare a product with a positive factor using the other factor's position relative to one, without performing the indicated multiplication.
Explain shrinking, unchanged size, and enlargement with a diagram or a quantity interpretation; recognize whole-number enlargement as a familiar case.
Explain fraction equivalence by multiplying a/b by n/n = 1 for a positive integer n, giving (n times a)/(n times b) without changing the quantity.

nodes.name: Statistical questions and anticipated variability
nodes.description: A statistical question anticipates variability in the data collected to answer it, and its answer accounts for that variability. Identify the attribute and observational units, distinguish such questions from questions about a fixed fact, and recognize that a mean or proportion can summarize varying observations in one number.
criteria: Classify a question by explaining whether the relevant observations are expected to vary, rather than merely checking whether the question mentions a group.
Identify what would be observed or measured and describe the anticipated variation, including possible variation in repeated measurements of one object.
Explain how an answer, including a single-number summary, accounts for the variable observations rather than reporting an unrelated fixed fact.

nodes.name: Describing a measured attribute and its context
nodes.description: Describe a numerical data set by saying what attribute was measured or counted, for which objects or people, how it was measured or recorded, and in which units. Include the available instrument or method and precision, and retain the units when interpreting a summary.
criteria: Identify the attribute represented by the values and the objects or people to which those values refer.
Describe the stated measurement or recording method and precision; distinguish measured, counted, and self-reported values without inventing unavailable method details.
State the measurement units and use them when explaining what a numerical summary means.

nodes.name: Plane sections of solid figures
nodes.description: Describe the two-dimensional figure formed where a plane slices a solid, including right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids. Relate the section's edges and vertices to the faces and edges cut by the plane, and explain how changing the slice changes its shape.
criteria: Identify and sketch the section of a right rectangular prism, including a cube, for specified parallel and oblique slices.
Describe sections of right rectangular pyramids, including a plane parallel to the base and a plane through the apex, using the stated position of the slice.
Justify the section's shape from the solid's intersected faces and edges; distinguish a cross-section from a projection or an unfolded net.

nodes.name: Simulating compound chance events
nodes.description: Design and run a random simulation of a compound event. Choose a device and an outcome mapping that match the specified probabilities and dependence assumptions, define one complete trial and its success condition, repeat trials, and use the observed success frequency to approximate the probability.
criteria: Specify a suitable coin, spinner, dice, draw, or random-number model and justify its mapping to the situation, including independence or replacement when appropriate.
Define one complete trial, its stopping rule, and the compound event being counted, including a waiting-time event.
Generate and record many trials, calculate successes divided by completed trials, and interpret the result as an approximate probability that can vary across runs.

edges.scope: extending half- and quarter-unit display construction to eighth-unit plots and addition/subtraction questions
edges.rationale: The Measurement Data Progression extends fractional ruler-data displays to addition and subtraction problems using half-, quarter-, and eighth-unit measurements. Earlier fractional-inch measurement and plotting is useful preparation, but the later display can also be introduced from a supplied measurement list.

edges.scope: collecting whole-unit length measurements before plotting their frequencies
edges.rationale: Measuring whole centimeters with a ruler supplies an immediate example of the measurements used in a whole-unit line plot. IM Hand Span Measures uses that activity. This is preparation, since the defined collection and plotting action can also be learned with another whole length unit.

edges.scope: reading half-inch and quarter-inch ruler marks and line-plot scales
edges.rationale: Understanding equal parts of a unit helps a learner read half- and quarter-inch tick marks. This supports the fractional measurement action without claiming that fractional ruler readings are needed for whole-unit plots.

edges.scope: extending the one-mark-per-observation display from whole-unit to fractional-inch measurements
edges.rationale: The Measurement Data Progression introduces whole-unit displays before extending the measurement scale to halves and quarters. The earlier action establishes numerical spacing and stacked observations; a fractional display can also be taught directly.

edges.scope: like-denominator addition and subtraction cases whose result does not exceed one unit
edges.rationale: The Chinese procedure supplies these elementary calculations after measurements are read from the plot. Its result-at-most-one restriction covers only part of the additive plotting action, so it is scoped preparation rather than a complete substitute or universal requirement.

edges.scope: extending fractional measurement plots from like-denominator addition/subtraction to other fraction operations
edges.rationale: The Measurement Data Progression develops additive interpretation before extending line-plot questions to unlike denominators, fraction products, limited fraction division, and equal redistribution. The earlier action is useful preparation, not a requirement to complete every earlier plotting activity.

edges.scope: measurement-plot questions with a chain of fraction additions and subtractions, including parentheses
edges.rationale: cnm_p174 specifically evaluates mixed addition/subtraction chains and parentheses. It can support a multi-step calculation after the plotted quantities are interpreted, but is not the basic like-denominator skill or a prerequisite for all plotting and arithmetic questions.

edges.scope: grade-5 measurement-plot questions whose sums or differences have unlike fractional denominators
edges.rationale: The grade-5 arithmetic procedure supplies this calculation technique. The Measurement Data Progression connects existing fraction arithmetic with line-plot data problems; the generic arithmetic node does not itself assess data interpretation.

edges.scope: finding a fractional measurement total from a repeated value and its plotted frequency
edges.rationale: Multiplying the repeated fractional amount by the observed count supports the total calculation. Repeated addition is also possible, so prior mastery of this multiplication procedure is not a strict requirement.

edges.scope: grade-5 questions applying fraction multiplication to measurement-plot data
edges.rationale: The existing fraction-product algorithm supports the arithmetic in the grade-5 branch after the plotted quantities are interpreted. It is preparation for that branch, not a prerequisite for constructing or reading the display.

edges.scope: sharing a plotted fractional total equally among a whole-number count of containers
edges.rationale: The general procedure for dividing fractions by integers supports equal sharing of a plotted fractional total. The grade-5 data problem may instead use a drawing or decomposition into unit fractions, so this is preparation and does not extend grade 5 to a general division algorithm.

edges.scope: the grade-5 whole-number divided by unit-fraction cases arising from measurement-plot questions
edges.rationale: The existing general fraction-division procedure includes these limited calculation cases. Only that subset prepares this branch; general fraction-by-fraction division is not required by grade 5 or by every line-plot activity.

edges.scope: recognizing cubes as the repeated solid units in a volume packing
edges.rationale: Prior recognition of cubes provides concrete shapes to pack and count. It does not establish volume measurement and is preparation rather than a requirement for learning the packing definition directly.

edges.scope: developing the rectangular-prism formula from rows and layers of cubes
edges.rationale: IM grade 5 Unit 1 and the Measurement Progression develop counting and layers before generalizing to length times width times height. That is a supported curricular route; evaluating an already-given formula does not logically require prior packing activities.

edges.scope: calculating the constituent rectangular-prism volumes from their dimensions
edges.rationale: The defined procedure explicitly calculates each constituent prism from its dimensions before adding. The existing rectangular-prism volume procedure supplies this calculation. Counting a cube model is an alternative introduction and does not make the formula a requirement for every possible demonstration of additivity.

edges.scope: understanding why disjoint parts contribute additive volumes
edges.rationale: Disjoint cube counts make additivity visible and prepare the decomposition procedure. IM Unit 1 introduces this observation before applying formulas to composite solids; formula-based application can also be taught directly.

edges.scope: interpreting a fractional multiplier as a specified number of equal parts of a quantity
edges.rationale: Explaining what it means to take a fractional multiple uses the meaning of a fraction as equal parts. The computational rules for multiplying fractions are not required for predicting product size without calculation.

edges.scope: locating a positive fractional multiplier below, at, or above one
edges.rationale: Recognizing proper and improper fractions supplies familiar comparisons with one that support predicting whether scaling shrinks or enlarges a quantity. These comparisons can also be developed within the scaling activity, so this is preparation rather than a required classification procedure.

edges.scope: reinterpreting the familiar equivalent-fraction rule as multiplication by one
edges.rationale: Knowing that multiplying numerator and denominator by the same positive integer preserves a fraction gives a familiar fact to explain as scaling by n/n. The scaling explanation can also develop that fact, so this is preparation rather than a mandatory proof order.

edges.scope: posing a question that variable data can answer at the start of a statistical investigation
edges.rationale: The Statistics and Probability Progression begins investigation with a question and anticipated variability. This sharpens the question-formulation step in the existing investigation-process node; familiarity with the whole process can also be acquired first.

edges.scope: identifying whether values came from a questionnaire, observation, experiment, or consulted source
edges.rationale: Recognizing data-collection methods helps a learner accurately describe how an attribute was recorded. The existing node does not itself require a precise attribute-and-unit statement, and such statements can be learned from a supplied data description without prior study of all collection methods.

edges.scope: tracing a prism section through its faces and edges
edges.rationale: Familiarity with a cube's or rectangular prism's faces and edges supports tracing the cut boundary. IM Cube Ninjas also allows physical models to develop this visualization, so prior mastery of the elementary solid-features node is useful preparation rather than an absolute requirement.

edges.scope: interpreting the simulated success proportion as an approximate probability
edges.rationale: The simulation procedure uses repeated-trial relative frequency to estimate the target probability. This inference is exactly the existing frequency-estimation concept. Tree-diagram rules for theoretical compound probabilities are not required: IM Waiting Times explicitly uses simulation before students know those rules.

reviews.coverageReason: The prior gap was the measurement-frequency display, not ordinary length measurement. The whole-unit line-plot action covers generating measurements, including repeated measurements, and displaying one observation per stacked mark. Fractional-inch collection and later fractional arithmetic have distinct actions and direct alignments. cnm_p040 covers a centimeter ruler example; cnm_p175 and cnm_294 are connected time-trend graphs, not this display.

sources.note: The standard explicitly combines collecting lengths, including repeated measurement, with a whole-number horizontal line-plot scale.
IM Hand Span Measures rounds ruler measurements to whole centimeters and records each with a mark above the corresponding scale value.
Saved Marble topic mt_mayItsxMUu, Measuring & Plotting Lengths, matches shortened ccss-math:2.MD.9. Its criteria include collecting lengths and a whole-unit line plot.

alignments.reason: Covers generating whole-unit length measurements and constructing their whole-number line plot, including repeated measurements of one object. Fractional acquisition and arithmetic are separate mathematical actions.

reviews.coverageReason: The fractional-inch measurement action supplies half/quarter-inch ruler readings and their appropriately marked line plot. Unit-fraction recognition supports the scale but does not by itself cover collecting or plotting these measurements. This action is distinct from whole-unit acquisition and later plot-based arithmetic.

sources.note: The standard requires measurements with rulers marked in half and quarter inches and a line plot using whole, half, or quarter units. IM lists no task here.
Measurement Data, PDF pages 10-11: grade 3 extends the grade-2 display using fractional ruler readings, with repeated observations stacked at their values.
Saved Marble topic mt_ghK1mnEstc, Halves and quarters (age 8+), matches shortened ccss-math:3.MD.4 and explicitly combines fractional-inch measurement with plotting.

alignments.reason: Covers generating measurements with rulers marked in half and quarter inches and plotting those measurements on an appropriate whole-, half-, or quarter-inch scale.

reviews.coverageReason: The additive measurement-plot action constructs half-, quarter-, and eighth-unit displays and solves addition/subtraction questions from their values and frequencies. Fractions are expressed in a common plotted unit for like-denominator arithmetic. General fraction algorithms remain scoped preparation; cnm_p080 alone is too narrow because its Chinese definition limits results to at most one. Later fraction products and division belong to a distinct action.

sources.note: The objective contains both half/quarter/eighth-unit displays and addition/subtraction problems using their data.

IM Button Diameters contrasts eighth-inch and quarter-inch plots. Its commentary says the printed task needs added operations questions to address the rest of the standard, and identifies like-denominator arithmetic for grade 4.
PDF page 11 permits relabeling the measurement scale in eighths to obtain like denominators when adding or subtracting the plotted fractional measurements.
Saved Marble topic mt_42QD6nYjiZ, Measurement Line Plots, matches ccss-math:4.MD.4. Its evidence includes totals and longest-minus-shortest differences.

alignments.reason: Includes both constructing the required fractional measurement display and solving contextual addition/subtraction questions with like-denominator amounts in halves, quarters, or eighths.

reviews.coverageReason: The fraction-operation measurement-plot action constructs the required fractional displays and solves questions from their values and frequencies using addition/subtraction, fraction products, limited fraction division, and equal redistribution. Existing general fraction algorithms remain scoped preparation rather than direct practice alignments. The whole-unit, fractional-inch acquisition, and additive plot actions retain separate direct alignments to their own standards.

sources.note: The standard uses fraction operations for the grade with measurement-plot data, including the example of equal redistribution across beakers.
PDF page 11 connects grade-5 fraction arithmetic to line-plot problems and equal redistribution; interpreting redistribution as a mean is identified as later grade-6 work.
IM Fractions on a Line Plot practices fraction sums and an eighth-unit scale, but explicitly uses card sums rather than measurement data, so that task alone does not establish full scope.
Saved Marble topic mt_IHipFGTFEY, Line plots with fractions, matches ccss-math:5.MD.2; its evidence includes measurement totals and equal redistribution.

alignments.reason: Includes constructing half-, quarter-, and eighth-unit measurement plots and using their data for the stated fraction operations and equal redistribution. Division uses the permitted unit-fraction/whole-number cases, with other fractional-total sharing explained through unit-fraction decomposition or drawings.

reviews.coverageReason: The previous units/formulas nodes did not define volume by a complete cube packing. The shared unit-cube node now explicitly states the no-gap/no-overlap condition and n cubes giving n cubic units, and also carries the closely connected counting procedure used by 5.MD.C.4.

sources.note: The standard's part b defines volume through a gapless, non-overlapping packing by n unit cubes; this is different from a conversion or formula rule.
Grade 5 Unit 1, Section A treats the unit-cube meaning and counting together; the narrative later develops prism formulas from layers.
Saved Marble topic mt_IuHa5UI5od, What volume means, matches ccss-math:5.MD.3.b, including the alternate dotted child suffix. Its definition contains the packing meaning.

alignments.reason: Contains the full packing definition and additionally measures volume through cube counts in named and improvised cubic units.

reviews.coverageReason: The new unit-cube node supplies counting as measurement and explicitly includes cubic centimeters, inches, feet, and improvised cube units. cnm_p162's Chinese definition concerns cubic-unit naming/conversion and cnm_p163 uses formulas, so neither is silently broadened to claim this previously missing measuring procedure.

sources.note: The standard explicitly measures by counting unit cubes and includes standard and improvised units.
PDF pages 26-27 develop volume measurement by packing, counting, and mentally organizing cubes into rows and layers before generalizing formulas.
Saved Marble topic mt_d7XktBQPxm, Counting Unit Cubes, matches ccss-math:5.MD.4; its evidence includes hidden cubes and recording the cubic unit.

alignments.reason: Covers all listed counting units and also makes the underlying packing definition explicit; that concept is separately stated in 5.MD.C.3.

reviews.coverageReason: The new additive-volume procedure fills the missing decomposition-and-addition step for two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms, including contextual application. Existing cnm_p163 is reused for each constituent prism. cnm_h107 only identifies constituents of composite solids and does not calculate their combined volume.

sources.note: Part c requires volume additivity for solids composed of two non-overlapping rectangular prisms and real-world use.
Grade 5 Unit 1, Section C applies the earlier prism-volume work to composite figures; it does not make every earlier curricular activity a strict prerequisite.
Saved Marble topic mt_5TBUFnCy5-, Volume as additive, matches ccss-math:5.MD.5.c; it splits an L-shaped solid and sums the prism volumes.

alignments.reason: Explicitly assesses the full two-prism decomposition, non-overlap condition, volume sum, explanation, and contextual application.

reviews.coverageReason: The shared scaling concept fills the missing reasoning without computing products. It covers the full parent, including both product-size comparison and explaining enlargement/shrinking and equivalence through multiplication by one. Existing fraction algorithms and cnm_p167 alone cover calculations or the equivalence fact, not this interpretation.

sources.note: The parent includes parts a and b, so coverage must include explanations and equivalence through multiplication by one, not only a product comparison.
IM Scaling Up and Down asks for distance comparisons using 6/4 and 3/4, explanations of shrinking/enlargement, and why multiplying by 4/4 preserves the distance.
Saved Marble topic mt_VKW8lOcFaw, Multiplication as scaling, matches ccss-math:5.NF.5, 5.NF.5.a, and 5.NF.5.b; it explicitly includes the multiplication-by-one equivalence link.

alignments.reason: Covers comparison without computation and both explanatory parts, including fraction equivalence. The positive-quantity condition states the domain under which strict increase/decrease claims hold.

reviews.coverageReason: The new shared scaling concept explicitly compares product and factor from the other factor's size without performing the multiplication. Existing cnm_p177/cnm_p178 are computation procedures and do not establish that reasoning. The same node is reused for the parent rather than creating a child-specific duplicate.

sources.note: Part a explicitly compares sizes based on the other factor and rules out calculating the indicated product as the intended method.
The task first compares running distances from the scaling factors before a common baseline distance is supplied.
Saved Marble topic mt_VKW8lOcFaw matches the alternate child code ccss-math:5.NF.5.a and includes predicting a product comparison before calculation.

alignments.reason: Contains the entire comparison-without-calculation objective and also the explanatory and equivalence scope of part b.

reviews.coverageReason: The new statistical-question concept fills the previous missing criterion of anticipated variability and accounting for it in an answer. cnm_300 lists the investigation process and cnm_292 chooses collection methods, but neither Chinese definition distinguishes statistical questions by variability. A single-number summary is not mistaken for a fixed-fact question.

sources.note: The standard defines statistical questions by anticipated variability and answers that account for it.
IM Identifying Statistical Questions treats questions about average dog ages and a school preference proportion as statistical, while a fixed count of bricks is not.
PDF page 4 includes variability in repeated measurements of one object, so variation need not come only from different people.
Saved Marble topic mt_iykH2P5oFq, Statistical questions, matches ccss-math:6.SP.1. It warns that a summary may be one number and that merely mentioning a group is insufficient.

alignments.reason: Explicitly recognizes anticipated variability, distinguishes deterministic questions, and explains how the answer represents variable observations.

reviews.coverageReason: The new scoped data-context procedure supplies the previously absent attribute/method/unit statement. The existing collection-method and population nodes provide related context but do not themselves assess describing the numerical attribute and measurement units. Observation counts and full distribution summaries belong to other children and are not claimed by this review.

sources.note: Part b specifically describes the investigated attribute, how it was measured, and its units, distinct from part a's observation count and part c's quantitative summaries.
PDF page 6 places attribute and units within the contextual summary, illustrated by the animal-speed data set.
Saved Marble topic mt_6gpryAnpoZ, What was measured, and how, matches ccss-math:6.SP.5b, not 6.SP.5.b. It covers attribute, method/precision and units, and additionally the part-a count.

alignments.reason: Directly assesses the attribute, observational referents, available measurement/recording method, and units required by this child objective.

reviews.coverageReason: The new plane-section procedure explicitly fills the missing slice-to-plane relationship for rectangular prisms and rectangular pyramids. cnm_051 covers projections and nets, cnm_p160 and cnm_h105 cover solid features, and none of their Chinese criteria assess sections. The existing dihedral-angle definition mentions a measuring section but not the shapes formed by general solid slices.

sources.note: The standard names plane sections of right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids as examples of the solid-to-plane relationship.

IM Cube Ninjas includes rectangular, triangular, and pentagonal slices and permits physical models. Its commentary explicitly does not require Pythagorean side lengths or exact intersection coordinates at grade 7.
Saved Marble topic mt_nRksLqt-iR, 3-D shapes (age 11+), matches ccss-math:7.G.3. It is broader than the standard, combining solid features, nets, and examples of cross-sections.

alignments.reason: Describes resulting two-dimensional shapes for specified planar slices, including both named types of solid, without adding a requirement for advanced spatial calculations.

reviews.coverageReason: The new simulation-design procedure fills the missing choice of random model, mapping, trial/stopping rule, and compound-event counting. cnm_288 already covers interpreting observed frequencies as probability estimates and is reused. cnm_287/cnm_311 enumerate theoretical outcomes, while cnm_298 selects survey samples. The supplementary cnm_315 designs games and checks fairness with trial frequencies, but does not explicitly model a target compound process or define complete waiting-time trials. None substitutes for the full simulation-design action.

sources.note: Part c asks for designing and using a simulation for compound-event frequencies, including a random-digit waiting-time example.

IM Waiting Times separates model assumptions, random outcomes, repeated trials, and approximate conclusions. It explicitly uses simulation before rules for theoretical compound probabilities are available.

PDF page 8 motivates simulation after probability basics for situations whose theoretical probabilities are not obvious. This supports a curricular preparation sequence without requiring tree-diagram mastery.

Saved Marble topic mt_nzdtOLXWWa, Simulating chance events, matches ccss-math:7.SP.8c. Its criteria include probability-matched random-digit mapping, complete waiting-time trials, and relative-frequency estimates.

alignments.reason: Designs the random process, defines compound-event trials, generates their frequencies, and interprets the probability estimate, including the waiting-time form in the standard.

companionReviews.coverageReason: The existing cnm_p167 states fraction equivalence but does not explain why fractional multipliers enlarge or shrink a positive quantity or connect equivalence to multiplication by one. The shared scaling concept supplies those explanations. It also assesses the comparison-without-computation objective in part a, so its link to part b is broader and the conservative coverage status remains partial.

sources.note: Part b requires explaining enlargement and shrinking under fractional multiplication and connecting equivalent fractions with multiplying by one. The comparison objective of part a is separately stated.
IM Scaling Up and Down includes an explanation of multiplication producing a smaller quantity and an explanation of fraction equivalence through a multiplier equal to one.

alignments.reason: Contains the full enlargement, shrinking, and multiplication-by-one explanations required by part b, together with the separate product-comparison action of part a.
